nodes.title: Part 1: Key Ideas
nodes.content: Quick primer on Part 1. Tap to flip cards covering the most-asked exam ideas in this domain.

flashcards.front: You are initializing a new Kubernetes control plane with kubeadm. You want the A?
flashcards.back: --apiserver-advertise-address tells kubeadm which IP address the API server should advertise to members of the cluster. --apiserver-bind-address controls which interface it binds to. --control-plane-endpoint is used for HA setups with a load balancer DNS/VIP. --node-ip is a kubelet flag, not a kubeadm init flag.

flashcards.front: A worker node needs to join an existing cluster but the bootstrap token has expi?
flashcards.back: 'kubeadm token create --print-join-command' creates a new bootstrap token and prints the complete 'kubeadm join' command including the token and CA cert hash. 'kubeadm token generate' only outputs a random token string — it does not register it with the cluster. The other options do not exist.

flashcards.front: You need to take a snapshot backup of etcd running as a static pod. The etcd dat?
flashcards.back: etcdctl snapshot save requires the endpoint and TLS credentials (--cacert, --cert, --key) to connect to the running etcd cluster. Without TLS flags, etcdctl will be rejected. 'etcdctl backup' is an old v2 API syntax no longer used. Running via kubectl exec without passing the certs would also fail. --data-dir is not a valid flag for snapshot save.

flashcards.front: After restoring an etcd snapshot to a new data directory /var/lib/etcd-restore, ?
flashcards.back: etcd runs as a static pod managed by the kubelet. Its manifest at /etc/kubernetes/manifests/etcd.yaml defines both the --data-dir argument and the hostPath mount. You must update both the --data-dir flag value and the hostPath volume source to point to the restored directory. The kubelet detects the manifest change and restarts the pod automatically.

nodes.title: Part 2: Key Ideas
nodes.content: Quick primer on Part 2. Tap to flip cards covering the most-asked exam ideas in this domain.

flashcards.front: You need a DaemonSet to run on every node including control plane nodes, which h?
flashcards.back: Taints prevent pods from being scheduled unless the pod spec includes a matching toleration. To run on tainted control plane nodes, the DaemonSet's pod template must include a toleration with key 'node-role.kubernetes.io/control-plane' and effect 'NoSchedule'. nodeSelector selects by label, not taint, and wouldn't overcome the taint restriction.

flashcards.front: A Job must run exactly 6 pod completions with no more than 2 pods running at the?
flashcards.back: 'completions' sets how many successful pod completions are required for the Job to be considered finished. 'parallelism' caps the number of pods that can run simultaneously. Together, completions: 6 and parallelism: 2 will run 2 pods at a time until 6 succeed. 'replicas' and 'maxSurge' are Deployment fields. 'concurrencyPolicy' is a CronJob field.

flashcards.front: A pod is stuck in 'Pending' state. 'kubectl describe pod my-pod' shows: 'Warning?
flashcards.back: The scheduler checks that a node has enough allocatable memory to satisfy the pod's request. If no node has 8Gi free, the pod stays Pending indefinitely. The correct fixes are: add a larger node, or reduce the memory request if the application genuinely needs less. Tolerations bypass taints, not resource constraints. PriorityClass can preempt lower-priority pods but won't create memory that doesn't exist. Increasing only the limit doesn't change the request. or reduce the pod's memory request if the workload allows it

flashcards.front: You want a pod to prefer scheduling on nodes labeled 'disktype=ssd' but still sc?
flashcards.back: preferredDuringSchedulingIgnoredDuringExecution is a 'soft' affinity rule. The scheduler tries to place the pod on a matching node but falls back to other nodes if needed. nodeSelector and requiredDuringSchedulingIgnoredDuringExecution are hard constraints — the pod won't schedule if no matching node exists. Taints repel pods, not attract them.

nodes.title: Part 3: Key Ideas
nodes.content: Quick primer on Part 3. Tap to flip cards covering the most-asked exam ideas in this domain.

flashcards.front: You deploy a CNI plugin and observe that pods on different nodes cannot communic?
flashcards.back: Intra-node pod communication working but cross-node failing is a classic CNI routing issue. The CNI plugin (Calico, Flannel, Weave, etc.) is responsible for establishing routes between nodes so pods on different nodes can reach each other. Issues include BGP peering failures (Calico), VXLAN setup failures (Flannel), or missing routes in the OS routing table. kube-proxy handles Service routing, not pod-to-pod communication.

flashcards.front: A PersistentVolumeClaim is stuck in 'Pending' state. 'kubectl describe pvc my-pv?
flashcards.back: A PVC binds either to a dynamically provisioned volume (requires a storageClassName referencing a StorageClass with a provisioner) or to a static PV that matches the claim's access mode, capacity, and any label selectors. With no storageClassName and no matching PV, the PVC cannot be bound. Setting storageClassName: '' explicitly opts out of dynamic provisioning. or a pre-existing PV that satisfies the claim's access mode and capacity

flashcards.front: A PersistentVolume is created with accessModes: [ReadWriteOnce] and capacity: 10?
flashcards.back: Kubernetes binds a PVC to a PV if the PV's access modes are a superset of the claim's, and the PV capacity is greater than or equal to the requested amount. The PV is not resized — the PVC gets access to the full 10Gi volume even though it only requested 5Gi. This is why over-provisioning is possible with static PVs.

flashcards.front: You need a volume that is shared between two containers in the same pod and is d?
flashcards.back: emptyDir is an ephemeral volume created when a pod is assigned to a node and deleted when the pod is removed. It is shared between all containers in the pod, making it ideal for inter-container communication or scratch space. hostPath persists on the node after pod deletion. PVCs persist independently. configMap mounts read-only configuration data.

nodes.title: Part 4: Key Ideas
nodes.content: Quick primer on Part 4. Tap to flip cards covering the most-asked exam ideas in this domain.

flashcards.front: You need to check why the kube-controller-manager is continuously restarting. Wh?
flashcards.back: 'kubectl logs --previous' (or -p) retrieves the logs from the previously terminated container instance. This is essential for CrashLoopBackOff diagnostics — the current container may not have any useful logs yet. 'kubectl describe pod' shows events but not the full log output. journalctl is for systemd services; as a static pod, the controller-manager logs are accessed via kubectl.

flashcards.front: A node's disk pressure condition is True. You run 'kubectl describe node worker-?
flashcards.back: DiskPressure is triggered when the kubelet detects available disk space on the node falls below the eviction threshold (default: imagefs.available < 15%). Common culprits are accumulated container images, large log files, or application data. Remediation includes: 'crictl rmi --prune' to remove unused images, cleaning old logs, or expanding the disk. The kubelet evicts pods to free up space.

flashcards.front: You observe that a pod is being evicted every few hours. 'kubectl describe pod' ?
flashcards.back: Pods without resource requests are treated as BestEffort QoS class, which is the first to be evicted under memory pressure. Setting memory requests elevates the pod to Burstable QoS (or Guaranteed if requests equal limits), making it harder to evict. PodDisruptionBudgets protect against voluntary disruptions. Running in kube-system does not grant eviction immunity based on namespace alone. and use a PodDisruptionBudget to protect it from eviction

flashcards.front: After applying a new NetworkPolicy, pods in namespace 'app' can no longer reach ?
flashcards.back: If a NetworkPolicy selects a pod and includes 'policyTypes: Egress', all egress is blocked unless explicitly allowed. DNS queries go to port 53 on the CoreDNS service. You must add an egress rule allowing UDP and TCP on port 53, either to the kube-system namespace or to the specific CoreDNS IP. Without this, DNS resolution breaks for the selected pods.
